chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
title: The union agent and the policeman who called Iller a creole
summary: Parker Berry's worry about a mixed band is realised when the union agent and officer question Iller, and Fields settles it by saying he looks white but is creole.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: So I said what. So I said we'll figure out something.
When we were first figuring to go south, Parker Berry--

Parker, when we were fixing to go, he said I don't know if you can; I said what. So he said something about Nat King and some concert and they stopped him because he had a mixed band or something, and he said you didn't say anything about that and I said no, oh Parker.

So anyway, when we were on the bandstand there, the union man, the business agent came around and he was white. Parker's star word used to be, 'Jesus, what now?' So this guy came in and he was smiling, this business agent, he wanted to check our card and

Parker goes, 'Oh, Jesus,' and so anyway he checked everybody's card but nobody had nothing about no race on the card, it just had the number and the local and whether the card is paid up or not. So he looked over all the cards and went on about his business.
So I got to bragging to Parker and said, what are you worrying about, everything is all right, and he says, well, maybe so; just like that.

So this union guy went on off and he just stood around. So when the dance kicked off, I guess this officer's that's going to be on duty during the day and the officer walked in, and when this officer walked in they almost got in a huddle and were almost hugging and kissing and they were talking and you could see them looking at the band and see them talking. So nobody said anything to them and when it came intermission, I went off--see, I was the road manager, so I went up to the box office to see how things were going and I got off the band-
stand and started to the box office and they started to cross the floor to meet me. I was like Parker and I said oh my God.

And so they got there and this union guy and the policeman weren't saying anything, they were just looking. He had a big, ten gallon hat on and this union guy says you've been here before, haven't you Fields? I said yes. I believe I like the band better than then, you got a nice group of guys and he was just talking, but you know he ain't saying what he wants to say. He was just saying one thing or another about the band and how's everything and of course I got kind of nervous, almost started to walk off from him and he goes, you know, this officer and I were just saying I'll be damned if that creole doesn't look like a white boy to me. I said he looks just like one.
I oftened wondered if this white guy, as a white musician is going to give me any

trouble and I said, yeah, that creole does look like one. So we went on and said I had a creole up there. And they said that creole just looks like a white boy, and I said yeah, he sure does look like one.
